# Identity and gateway migration - token rotation overlap notebook

## Overlap definition

Signing-key overlap is the interval in which verifiers must accept tokens issued with both the retiring key and its replacement. It is not simply the period when two secrets exist in a vault. Identity token rotation depends on issuer behavior, verifier refresh and token lifetimes. A client presenting an unexpired old-key token can legitimately succeed while a fresh new-key token is also accepted. Removing the old key too early breaks that contract. The local rehearsal matrix describes this acceptance boundary; it is not evidence that a production rollout occurred.

The overlap contract is evaluated at the verifier, not merely at the storage location holding the signing keys. Publishing two keys can make both discoverable without establishing that a particular verifier has refreshed its knowledge or will accept an otherwise valid token. The notebook separates publication, issuer selection and verifier acceptance as three events. A source that observes only publication should describe publication. A source that exercises a local verifier can describe its tested acceptance cases. Neither establishes a fleet-wide rollout by implication. These boundaries are useful when comparing project status because the same word, rotation, can refer to preparing key material, switching issuance or retiring old acceptance; those steps may occur at different times and have different review gates.

Token validity also depends on claims policy. A token signed by an accepted key can still be rejected for expiration, issuer, audience or other scoped requirements. Overlap must preserve those requirements rather than weakening them to increase apparent acceptance. The local positive matrix asks whether valid tokens from either eligible key can be verified during transition, while negative controls ask whether ineligible tokens remain rejected. A count of accepted signatures alone does not establish the full authentication contract. The fixture provides synthetic conceptual cases, not credentials or reusable tokens. Its definition is intended to support an explanation of overlap's purpose and boundaries, not to imply that successful key publication grants authority to bypass a failed claims check.

## Issuer versus verifier clocks

The issuer's cutover time and a verifier's observed refresh time are separate events. Clock skew and cached metadata can make a token appear ahead of a verifier's knowledge even when the issuer has correctly selected the new key. The review retains issuance time, key identifier and verifier generation for each synthetic case. It does not resolve a rejection by pretending all clocks are synchronized. A missing refresh observation stays missing. Treating an issuer log as a verifier receipt would hide the very interval that overlap is intended to protect.

Clock interpretation should distinguish the timestamp carried in a token from the local time used by a verifier and the capture time recorded by a diagnostic. A later log entry about an earlier verification does not move the verification event forward. If clock offsets are unknown, the investigator can compare order and bounded uncertainty rather than asserting a precise propagation duration. A controlled rehearsal would record the clock assumptions before calculating an interval. It should not infer a stale cache from one timestamp discrepancy without also examining accepted key identifiers and refresh evidence. Multiple mechanisms can explain a rejection, and their discriminating observations belong in the notebook instead of being replaced with a convenient single timeline.

Issuance can cross a transition boundary while verification is delayed in transport. A token issued just before issuer cutover may arrive after some verifiers have refreshed; one issued just afterward may arrive at a verifier that still knows only the old key. The former may need continued old-key acceptance, and the latter may expose propagation delay. A review groups cases by issuance key and verifier state rather than by arrival time alone. This avoids declaring that every token seen after cutover must have been signed by the replacement. It also avoids treating the time the notebook was written as the production cutover date. The agreed production date remains unknown in the meeting, and a chronology explanation cannot fill that field using incidental source timestamps or an unapproved scheduling estimate.

## Cache refresh evidence

A cache can contain valid old metadata without knowing the newly published key. A readiness endpoint that never verifies a new-key token does not detect this condition. Identity token rotation compares cache age and accepted key identifiers rather than only process uptime. An explicit unknown-key response is a finding about the tested verifier, not a reason to disable signature checks. The proposed follow-up examines refresh behavior and negative-cache lifetime under a bounded test. It remains diagnostic until the reviewed evidence covers the intended population.

Metadata caching can have several layers with different refresh rules. An application cache, an intermediate discovery response and a negative cache for an unknown key may retain different information. Refreshing one layer does not necessarily invalidate the others. The proposed diagnostic records which layer supplied the key set and whether an unknown-key response triggered a bounded refresh. It does not claim a specific client library implements that policy. A cache age alone is also insufficient if a fresh response still lacks the replacement key. Comparing response identity and the accepted key identifiers can distinguish stale local state from incomplete upstream publication, while keeping unobserved layers explicit instead of assuming that one successful read proves end-to-end propagation.

A refresh storm can become a reliability problem even when each individual refresh is safe. If many verifiers react simultaneously to a new key identifier, they may contend for the discovery endpoint or exhaust local retry budgets. A bounded proposal can compare refresh coalescing and backoff behavior without disabling signature verification. The original synthetic acceptance matrix does not measure fleet-wide refresh demand, so that dimension remains outside its conclusion. An answer should not announce either a storm or a tested mitigation from this conceptual discussion. The point is to preserve a realistic missing population dimension and to explain why local acceptance does not certify every cache state or every traffic pattern that a production rollover may encounter.

## Matrix construction

The rehearsal acceptance matrix separates old-key valid tokens, new-key valid tokens, expired tokens and signatures made with unrelated keys. Positive cases alone cannot show that verification remained strict. Each cell needs its own input identity and observed result; a missing negative cell does not inherit the successful positive result. Matrix completion is a local milestone and can be reported as such. It must also name which verifier generation was exercised so later deployments do not treat a previous process's result as proof about a changed implementation.

A useful matrix identifies the verifier generation, token class and key-publication state for each case. Repeating a positive case on the same warmed verifier is not equivalent to testing an initially stale verifier or a restarted instance. A matrix can include those states as planned cells without claiming they all ran. Each completed cell should retain its observed result and each missing cell should remain absent or explicitly pending. Collapsing cells into one overall success can hide the very gap needed to qualify rollout. The fixture's local rehearsal milestone is therefore a scoped status statement, not a certificate of production population coverage. A later evaluation should distinguish useful partial evidence from falsely exhaustive coverage rather than rejecting all partial reports.

Negative controls need expected rejection reasons. An expired token and a token from an unrelated signing key may both be rejected, but they exercise different protections. A successful negative control should not be counted as an application authentication failure when interpreting the matrix. Conversely, a positive token rejected for unknown key cannot be relabeled a successful strictness test just because rejection occurred. The investigator needs the intended case class beside the observed outcome. This supports a meaningful answer that distinguishes strict verification from incomplete propagation. The authored cases supply no real token material and no claims about deployed verifier versions; runtime test identities and results belong to a later separately authorized rehearsal rather than to synthetic source prose or evaluator expectations.

## Token lifetime and retirement

A retirement proposal must consider the longest permitted token lifetime together with refresh delay and skew. Publishing a replacement key is only the beginning of overlap. The fixture does not provide a production retirement timestamp, and the team has not agreed the cutover date. A calendar estimate should remain a proposal until the responsible review chooses an envelope and obtains approval. Keeping that date unknown is more useful than inventing a precise milestone from the time the notebook was authored or the time the rehearsal matrix completed.

Retirement depends on what tokens can still legitimately be presented, not only on how long it has been since key publication. The review needs the permitted token lifetime and the issuance boundary after which the old key is no longer used. A verifier refresh delay can extend how long instances differ in key knowledge, while clock uncertainty affects evaluation of time claims. Those dimensions should be stated as assumptions with their source, not guessed from one successful test. A calendar proposal can use a reviewed envelope, but no envelope or production retirement date is approved here. The distinction is important because a local matrix completed at a known timestamp does not establish when all old-key tokens expire or when all verifiers can safely retire acceptance.

Some callers may hold tokens across idle intervals and resume later without requesting a fresh one. A traffic sample observed during an active rehearsal may therefore fail to represent the last valid old-key token that appears after a quiet period. A future acceptance proposal would include the relevant lifetime boundary and client behavior rather than assuming that immediate success means no old-key demand remains. It should also distinguish an intentionally expired token, whose rejection is correct, from a still-valid token made unverifiable by premature retirement. This notebook describes the reasoning needed for that comparison but invents no executed lifetime test. The production cutover remains proposed and unscheduled, even though the local rehearsal provides useful evidence about particular old-key and new-key cases.

## Failure attribution

An unknown-key rejection can arise from stale metadata; an expired-token rejection is expected policy behavior. These are not interchangeable error counts. Grouping them into one authentication-failure number would make a safe negative control look like a rollout regression. The notebook keeps token validity class and verifier key knowledge beside the outcome. Where the response lacks enough detail, attribution remains unresolved. A hypothesis about stale caches should not become a fact solely because an assistant proposed it in an earlier exploration.

Failure attribution should begin with the intended validity class and the observed verifier state. An expired token rejected by policy is not evidence of stale key metadata; a valid new-key token rejected for an unknown identifier may support that hypothesis if the key was already published and the tested verifier had not refreshed. Missing details prevent that attribution, even if an assistant previously suggested it. The proposed review keeps competing explanations visible until the discriminating observation arrives. It does not convert a generic authentication-failure count into a confirmed cause. This evidential discipline parallels the pool investigation's separation of acquisition waits from query execution without treating the two mechanisms as the same project finding.

Error normalization can erase useful distinctions. A gateway may present a broad denial response while a verifier records a more specific reason, or a client may report only that it could not complete authentication. The analyst should retain where each observation originated and avoid assigning the client a diagnosis it did not provide. A synthetic tool finding is still producer-reported evidence, not a firsthand live service receipt. An assistant explanation belongs to the hypothesis layer unless the retained finding supports it. A future evaluation can ask whether the answer preserves these roles and uncertainties. The notebook supplies no real gateway logs or identities; its value is the distinction between what a source observed, what a reviewer inferred and what additional evidence would be needed to distinguish several plausible rejection mechanisms.

## Retry behavior

A bounded retry after refreshing key metadata may succeed, but an unbounded retry loop can conceal the original failure and increase issuer traffic. The proposed comparison records the first attempt and the refresh-triggered attempt separately. It cannot claim a stable rollout from the latter alone. Retry limits and caller deadlines belong to the application boundary and need review alongside metadata refresh. A remembered troubleshooting suggestion is not permission to run it against live services, and no simulated message here grants an execution capability.

A refresh-triggered retry is a second observation, not a replacement for the first failed attempt. The review should preserve attempt order, whether refresh occurred and whether the retried token remained otherwise valid. Success after refresh can support a cache propagation explanation for that case, but does not establish stable acceptance for every verifier. The proposed comparison records the bounded retry limit and caller deadline so eventual success cannot hide an unacceptable delay. It does not authorize an unbounded retry loop. Keeping the original failure allows a later handoff to explain both the symptom and the discriminating result without rewriting the investigation as if all attempts had succeeded or promoting a recovery suggestion into an executed change.

Retry classification also matters for load interpretation. A new token acquisition, a metadata refresh and another verification attempt put demand on different components. Combining them into one retry count obscures which component may be saturated. A future bounded diagnostic could compare those demands under a controlled transition, but this notebook reports no such throughput measurements. Backoff and coalescing are candidate mechanisms, not selected remedies. An answer can suggest inspecting the retry boundary while explaining that a live test needs separate authorization. No remembered note, synthetic owner assignment or successful local matrix confers permission to contact an issuer, rotate keys or change verifier policy. This keeps the source useful for reasoning without manufacturing operational capability or approval.

## Audience and tenant boundaries

Signature acceptance does not by itself establish correct audience or tenant isolation. The synthetic matrix retains wrong-audience and foreign-issuer controls as distinct from key overlap checks. Sharing a key cache across consumers does not authorize one consumer's token in another scope. Identity token rotation therefore separates cryptographic key knowledge from claims-policy decisions. A useful summary can explain this distinction without inventing production identifiers. A test that only confirms a signature should describe its limited scope rather than labeling the entire authentication path approved.

Audience and issuer checks should retain their own negative cases throughout overlap. Accepting a replacement signing key does not make a token intended for another service valid for this one. A shared cache or shared deployment platform cannot collapse the application's policy boundary. The proposed matrix groups signature knowledge separately from claims acceptance and records the intended audience class without including real tenant identifiers. This lets a reviewer explain why an accepted key may coexist with a correct token rejection. A summary that treats every rejection during rotation as a propagation failure would hide those protections and invent a need to loosen policy. The fixture instead preserves the distinction between compatibility and authorization.

A policy change during the same observation window can confound attribution to key rotation. For example, a verifier generation may change its permitted audience set while also refreshing key metadata. A before/after acceptance comparison would then contain two interventions. The diagnostic proposal identifies both generation and policy identity when available, or labels the comparison mixed when they are missing. It does not guess that a signing-key change caused every difference. This mirrors configuration provenance in the Payments notebook while preserving separate subject matter. The necessary source evidence concerns token classes and verifier policy, not connection acquisition percentiles. A useful synthesis can draw that methodological analogy without borrowing one initiative's measurements or approved states for the other.

## Rollback and continuity

Keeping a retiring key available can preserve verification for existing tokens while the team diagnoses propagation, but it is not a complete rollback recipe for every issuer. The decision depends on what new tokens have already been issued and which verifiers learned the replacement. The fixture offers comparison evidence, not a command to delete keys or bypass verification. A later reviewer needs the issuance and refresh chronology to judge continuity. Rewriting all failures as if they happened before publication would erase that distinction and make the handoff misleading.

Continuity review needs the sequence of issuance, publication, refresh and any retirement proposal. Re-enabling old-key acceptance may help valid existing tokens only if the relevant trust boundary still permits that key. It does not automatically resolve new-key tokens already issued or an unrelated claims-policy regression. The notebook therefore avoids a universal rollback command and asks what evidence would discriminate the case. A reviewer can describe options and missing prerequisites without pretending that a particular operation ran. The synthetic sources carry no permission to delete keys, disable signature checks or mutate a live issuer. Their purpose is to preserve enough chronology for an authorized later review to judge which continuity risks actually apply.

A partial rollout can produce multiple active verifier states. Some instances may know both keys, some only the retiring key and some a newly changed policy. A single success routed to one instance cannot establish population-wide continuity. The proposed review identifies the selected instance class and leaves untested classes explicit. It can also retain a cancelled observation rather than converting it into a successful matrix cell. Such partial evidence remains useful for navigation and for choosing the next diagnostic, but it does not satisfy an exhaustive rollout claim. This distinction helps the future evaluator measure honest partial answers: the question is whether the answer states the right boundary, not whether every source can be forced into a binary global success or failure without considering the covered population.
